problem: Prior multi-agent visual exploration is either classical planning (frontier/RRT/Voronoi/APF), which is slow, needs tuning and has limited cooperation expressiveness, or end-to-end MARL, which is restricted to simple grid worlds or performs worse than planners and generalizes poorly across scenes and team sizes.
motivation: Multi-agent exploration should be much faster than single-agent, but learning cooperative strategies from visual input is hard due to large joint observation/action spaces, and RL policies generalize poorly to new scenes and team sizes. The authors extend the modular single-agent Active Neural SLAM (ANS) to multiple agents so that only a high-level global planner has to be learned.
key_idea: Replace ANS's global planner with an RL-trained, team-size-invariant Multi-agent Spatial Planner built on a hierarchical spatial/team transformer (Spatial-TeamFormer), plus map refiner/merger and per-scene policy distillation into a meta policy.
insight: Hierarchical attention that separates spatial encoding within each agent from cross-agent reasoning per grid cell beats flattened, unified, or pooled alternatives (Fig. 5-6 ablations: w.o. TeamFormer and Flattened perform worse, No Team Rel. Enc. has the worst overlap and steps). The hierarchical region+point action head handles multi-modal goal distributions better than a Gaussian over the map. Policy distillation from per-scene experts is essential for generalization: MAANS w.o. PD is worse than RRT/Voronoi on test scenes, while MAANS with PD beats all planning baselines.
method: Modular pipeline: reuses frozen ANS Neural SLAM and Local Policy; only the global planner MSP is trained with MAPPO (parameter shared, shared team reward).

CNN feature extractor: a weight-shared 5-layer CNN converts each agent's 6-channel global-frame map (obstacle, explored, position, decayed trajectory, last goal, goal history) into a G×G (G=8) feature map, with position, relative-coordinate and previous-goal embeddings.

Spatial-TeamFormer: stacked blocks (2 in the paper) of an Individual Spatial Encoder (self-attention over each agent's own G×G grid) and a Team Relation Encoder (per-grid self-attention across N agents); this gives O(N²G²+NG⁴) cost and is team-size invariant.

Action generator: hierarchical action space with a discrete region head (softmax over 8×8 regions) and a continuous point head (sigmoid-bounded x,y within the region), using features of the deciding agent.

Map refiner and merger: refiner composes past local maps into global maps, aligns them to a common frame, and crops/enlarges the explorable region; merger max-pools all agents' maps and is used only by the FMM local planner, not by MSP.
Policy distillation: train per-scene teacher policies (9 representative scenes, N=2), then distill into one student with DAgger-style imitation (KL on region, squared error on point).
Team reward: team and individual coverage reward, success bonus at 90%/95% coverage, overlap penalty, and time penalty.

setting.backbone: ANS Neural SLAM + local policy (frozen, reused) + MSP (CNN + Spatial-TeamFormer, trained with MAPPO and distilled)
setting.training_data: RL in Habitat on 23 Gibson training scenes (only 9 representative scenes used for per-scene teachers then distilled); 10^4 episodes per RL run, 3 seeds; N=2 (also N=3) agents
setting.observation: egocentric RGB per agent + noisy pose sensor, converted by Neural SLAM into 2D occupancy/explored maps; perfect communication between agents; birth locations known
setting.action_space: Discrete low-level Turn Left / Turn Right / Forward; global planner outputs a 2D long-term goal (region + point) every 15 steps, followed by FMM local planner and local policy
setting.privileged: none (agents know each other's birth locations and share maps via perfect communication)

numbers.eval_set_note: 10 testing scenes (filtered Gibson validation scenes plus 3 added middle scenes); 300 episodes (100 per seed)
numbers.extra: Trained on N=2; the testing scenes are unseen; Steps is steps to 90% coverage

numbers_note: This is not a VLN/ObjectNav benchmark; metrics are Coverage, Steps to 90% coverage, and Mutual Overlap on filtered Gibson scenes in Habitat. Many further tables (N=3 training, varying team size) are in the appendix and not all copied here.
results: MAANS reduces steps to 90% coverage by 20.56% on training scenes and 7.99% on testing scenes versus the best planning baseline at N=2 (158.55 vs RRT 199.59 on train; 144.16 vs Voronoi 156.68 on test). It also transfers zero-shot to N=3,4 and to varying team sizes, clearly beating baselines on training scenes and being comparable on test scenes.
limitations: Assumes perfect communication and a centralized planner, with agents knowing each other's birth positions.
Test-scene gains are small and sometimes worse than Voronoi at N=3,4 on test scenes, and mutual overlap is worse there; the setup requires per-scene teacher training, and only 9 scenes are used.
Only small Gibson scenes with up to 4 agents are evaluated, with no real robots and exploration only (no goal-directed tasks).
